title: Create in Me a Clean Heart
superscription: For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba.

verses.text: Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion; according to Your great compassion, blot out my transgressions.
Wash me clean of my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin.
For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.
Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight, so that You may be proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge.
Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me.
Surely You desire truth in the inmost being; You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.
Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.
Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones You have crushed rejoice.
Hide Your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities.
Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.
Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me.
Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit.
Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You.
Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, the God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing of Your righteousness.
O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare Your praise.
For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it; You take no pleasure in burnt offerings.
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.
In Your good pleasure, cause Zion to prosper; build up the walls of Jerusalem.
Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices, in whole burnt offerings; then bulls will be offered on Your altar.

context.author: The title names David. In Book Two, Psalms 51-65 are all “of David,” and several titles tie them to events in his life.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: The title places it “when Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba.” David had taken Uriah’s wife and arranged Uriah’s death (2 Samuel 11), and Nathan’s parable ended with “You are that man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). David asks for nothing but mercy: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion; according to Your great compassion, blot out my transgressions” (v.1). “Against You, You only, have I sinned” (v.4). He goes back to the root: “I was sinful when my mother conceived me” (v.5). “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow” (v.7). “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (v.10). He knows what God wants: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (v.17).
context.custom: Hyssop, a small bushy plant, was used to sprinkle blood or water in cleansing rites, for a healed leper or a person defiled by a corpse (Leviticus 14:4-7; Numbers 19:18), and at the first Passover (Exodus 12:22). The law offered no sacrifice for deliberate adultery and murder (Leviticus 20:10; Numbers 35:31), which is why David can only throw himself on God’s mercy. The last two verses, asking God to rebuild Jerusalem’s walls, may have been added when the psalm was used after the exile.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 52 is titled for Doeg the Edomite, who betrayed the priests of Nob.
context.timelineBible: Paul quotes v.4 in Romans 3:4: “So that You may be proved right when You speak.” The tax collector in Jesus’ parable prays in the spirit of this psalm: “God, have mercy on me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). Ezekiel promises, “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). It is the fourth of the seven penitential psalms, and the church sings it on Ash Wednesday.

translation.meaning: To wipe out, erase, as writing from a scroll.
Hyssop, a small plant used for sprinkling in cleansing rites.
To create; in the Bible only God is the subject of this verb (Genesis 1:1).
To break, shatter; a broken spirit.

gospelParallels.note: So that You may be proved right when You speak.
God, have mercy on me, a sinner.
He is faithful and just to forgive us.

otBackground.note: Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow.
A new heart and a new spirit.

overview.summary: After Nathan exposed his adultery and murder, David begs for mercy, owns his sin before God alone, and asks to be washed and given a clean heart and a willing spirit.

archaeology.t: The palace stood on the City of David, above the houses below.
A massive building on the City of David that some identify as David’s palace.

overview.discussion: “Against You, You only, have I sinned” (v.4). What changes when I see my sin first as against God, not just against people or rules?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-80 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David
overview.audience: God, against whom I have sinned

historicalImage.caption: Nathan and David, by Henri de Triqueti (1837). The prophet confronted the king over Bathsheba and Uriah: “You are that man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). Psalm 51 is titled for that moment.

currentImage.caption: The Stepped Stone Structure on the City of David, the hill David captured and made his capital (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Many archaeologists date it to the 10th or 9th century BC; the dating is debated.
